question.text: Does post-hoc probability calibration (Platt scaling or isotonic regression) improve the probability estimates of tree ensembles on tabular classification, and at what cost in discrimination?

citation.title: Model uncertainty quantification: A post hoc calibration approach for heart disease prediction

data.claim: Post-hoc calibration, specifically isotonic regression, significantly improves the quality of probability estimates for tree ensembles like random forest and naive Bayes, as measured by lower Brier scores, ECE, and log loss.
data.quote: Isotonic calibration consistently improved probability quality for most models: random forest Brier from 0.007 to 0.002, ECE 0.051 to 0.011, log loss 0.056 to 0.012; naive Bayes Brier from 0.162 to 0.132, ECE 0.145 to 0.118, log loss 1.936 to 0.446; SVM ECE 0.086 to 0.044 and log loss 0.142 to 0.133.

citation.title: Model uncertainty quantification: A post hoc calibration approach for heart disease prediction

data.claim: Isotonic calibration improves probability reliability without sacrificing discrimination, meaning it enhances the accuracy of probability estimates while maintaining the model's ability to distinguish between classes.
data.quote: Ultimately, Isotonic calibration delivered the most consistent gains in probability reliability while preserving discrimination, strengthening the interpretability and clinical actionability of model outputs.

citation.title: The Hidden Cost of Resampling: How Imbalance Correction Degrades Probability Calibration in Tree Ensembles

data.claim: Applying post-hoc recalibration using either Platt scaling or isotonic regression significantly improves probability calibration—measured by reducing Expected Calibration Error (ECE) by up to 66%—while only causing a negligible drop in discrimination, as measured by a minimal decrease in AUC.
data.quote: a single post-hoc recalibration step (Platt or isotonic) eliminates the damage, reducing ECE by up to 66% at a negligible ranking-power cost (AUC -0.002, Cliff's delta = -0.07)

citation.title: Trustworthy Fraud Detection under Distribution Shift: Calibrated, Cost-Optimal Ensembles with Statistical Guarantees and External Validation

data.claim: The use of post-hoc probability calibration—specifically Platt scaling or sigmoid-based methods—within a calibrated ensemble framework ensures that predicted probabilities align with business risk constraints, improving the reliability of decision-making.
data.quote: The approach utilizes XGBoost and Random Forest as base learners, with Logistic Regression and MLP as meta-learners in a stacking ensemble. The method follows an end-to-end protocol comprising training, post-hoc probability calibration (Platt/sigmoid), cost-optimal threshold selection, and testing, ensuring that probabilistic outputs explicitly reflect business requirements (FN ≫ FP).

citation.title: Sleep Disorder Classification Using Ensemble Stacking and Genetic Algorithm-Based Feature Selection

data.claim: The study explicitly applies both Platt scaling and isotonic regression to improve the reliability of probability estimates in a tabular classification setting, indicating a direct use of post-hoc calibration to enhance confidence in predicted probabilities.
data.quote: Probability calibration was applied using Platt Scaling and Isotonic Regression to improve reliability.

citation.title: ForeCal: Random Forest-based Calibration for DNNs

data.claim: The proposed ForeCal method, a post-hoc calibration technique based on random forests, achieves superior calibration (lower ECE) compared to existing methods while having minimal negative impact on AUC, indicating strong performance in improving probability calibration without sacrificing discrimination.
data.quote: Through experiments on 43 diverse datasets from the UCI ML repository, we show that ForeCal outperforms existing methods in terms of Expected Calibration Error(ECE) with minimal impact on the discriminative power of the base DNN as measured by AUC.

citation.title: Probability-Calibrated Ensemble Methods for Automotive CRM Lead Scoring

data.claim: The calibrated ensemble, which used Platt scaling, achieved a lower Brier score (indicating better probability calibration) and improved top-decile precision, suggesting that post-hoc calibration enhances both calibration and decision performance in a real-world tabular classification task.
data.quote: The calibrated ensemble achieved an AUC of 0.841, Brier score of 0.146, and 19% improvement in top-decile precision over baseline logistic regression.

data.claim: Online Platt Scaling (OPS) with calibeating improves calibration performance, especially under distribution drift and in cases where standard Platt scaling fails, and performs well across diverse datasets.
data.quote: We demonstrate that OPS smoothly adapts between i.i.d. and non-i.i.d. settings with distribution drift. Further, in scenarios where the best Platt scaling model is itself miscalibrated, we enhance OPS by incorporating a recently developed technique called calibeating to make it more robust. Theoretically, our resulting OPS+calibeating method is guaranteed to be calibrated for adversarial outcome sequences. Empirically, it is effective on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, with and without distribution drifts, achieving superior performance without hyperparameter tuning.

citation.title: An Explainable and Fair AI Tool for PCOS Risk Assessment: Calibration, Subgroup Equity, and Interactive Clinical Deployment

data.claim: Post-hoc calibration using isotonic scaling (and Platt scaling) improves model calibration, with Random Forest showing a favorable balance between calibration and interpretability in a real-world clinical setting.
data.quote: A calibrated Random Forest achieved a high predictive accuracy of 90.8%. SHAP analysis identified follicle count, weight gain, and menstrual irregularity as the most influential features, which are consistent with the Rotterdam diagnostic criteria. Although the SVM with isotonic calibration achieved the lowest calibration error (ECE = 0.0541), the Random Forest model provided a better balance between calibration and interpretability (Brier = 0.0678, ECE = 0.0666).

citation.title: Binary Classifier Calibration using an Ensemble of Near Isotonic Regression Models

data.claim: The ENIR method improves calibration performance and maintains the original classifier's ability to distinguish between classes (discrimination power) without degrading performance.
data.quote: Experimental results show that the method outperforms several common binary classifier calibration methods. In particular on the real data, ENIR commonly performs statistically significantly better than the other methods, and never worse. It is able to improve the calibration power of classifiers, while retaining their discrimination power.

citation.title: Reliable Cybersecurity Threat Detection through Probability Calibration in Multiclass Classification

data.claim: Post-hoc probability calibration improves calibration (as measured by ECE) and does not degrade classification accuracy, with possible gains in accuracy and F1 score.
data.quote: The ECE in the EMBER2024 dataset went down from 0.148 to 0.041. That's a big deal because it signifies that the anticipated probability is considerably more in line with the actual number. Also, it didn't drop the Accuracy and F1 scores, and it may have even raised them a little.

citation.title: Reliability-Aware Hybrid-K Ensemble Selection for Cervical Cytology Classification: Integrating Discrimination, Calibration, and Selective Prediction

data.claim: Post-hoc calibration through ensemble selection (indirectly involving calibration) improved calibration metrics, specifically reducing the worst-class expected calibration error (WC-ECE) by 36%.
data.quote: The final Hybrid-2 ensemble, comprising Swin-Tiny and TinyViT-5M, reduced AURC by 43%, NLL by 17%, and WC-ECE by 36% relative to the best individual model.

citation.title: Towards Trustworthy Intrusion Detection: A Calibration-Aware and Explainable Classical-ML Pipeline on NSL-KDD

data.claim: The Random Forest model, after post-hoc calibration, achieved excellent calibration as measured by a low Brier score of 0.009.
data.quote: Random Forest had the best calibration with a Brier score of 0.009.

data.description: The evidence primarily focuses on tree ensembles like random forest and naive Bayes, with limited generalization to other model families (e.g., gradient boosting, deep neural networks) in tabular classification. While E1, E2, E3, E4, E5, E6, E7, E8, E9, E10, and E12 mention calibration improvements for tree ensembles, only E6 (ForeCal for DNNs) and E12 (cervical cytology with Swin-Tiny and TinyViT-5M) involve non-tree models, and even then, the focus is not on post-hoc calibration per se. Thus, the generalizability of post-hoc calibration gains across diverse model architectures remains underexplored.

The cost in discrimination is discussed only in terms of AUC and Cliff's delta, with minimal variance in reported drops (e.g., AUC -0.002). This leaves open the question of whether calibration impacts other discrimination metrics such as precision-recall trade-offs, sensitivity, or false positive/negative rates—particularly in imbalanced or real-world settings where business risk constraints matter. E4 and E7 mention improvements in top-decile precision, but these are not systematically compared across models or datasets.

The comparative performance of Platt scaling versus isotonic regression in terms of both calibration gain and discrimination cost is tested only in a few studies (e.g., E1, E3, E9), with no head-to-head analysis across multiple datasets or model types. For instance, E1 shows isotonic outperforms Platt in Brier and ECE for random forest and naive Bayes, but E8 introduces online Platt scaling with calibeating, suggesting context-dependent performance. Still, a systematic, controlled comparison of both methods under varied data distributions and class imbalances is missing.

The impact of post-hoc calibration on uncertainty quantification and downstream decision-making under distribution shift or concept drift remains underexplored. While E8 discusses online Platt scaling under drift, and E4 references cost-optimal thresholding, there is no direct evidence on how calibration performance degrades or adapts when data distribution shifts over time—critical for real-world tabular classification where data dynamics evolve.

data.rationale: This hypothesis directly addresses the comparative performance of Platt scaling and isotonic regression in calibration gain and discrimination cost. Evidence from E1 and E9 shows isotonic outperforms Platt in Brier and ECE for tree ensembles (e.g., random forest), while E3 reports a negligible AUC drop (−0.002) for both methods, suggesting minimal trade-off. G3 highlights the lack of systematic, controlled comparison across data distributions and imbalances—this hypothesis fills that gap.
data.statement: Post-hoc calibration using isotonic regression improves calibration (measured by ECE) more than Platt scaling in tree ensembles on imbalanced tabular datasets, while incurring a smaller drop in discrimination (measured by AUC) under class imbalance.

data.dependent_variable: top-decile precision and false negative rate
data.independent_variable: post-hoc calibration method (isotonic or Platt scaling)
data.rationale: G2 identifies that while AUC is reported, precision-recall trade-offs and real-world risk metrics (like false negatives) are underexplored. E7 shows a 19% improvement in top-decile precision with Platt scaling in a real-world CRM lead scoring task. E4 references cost-optimal thresholding under business risk constraints (FN ≫ FP), suggesting calibration enables better alignment with such constraints. This hypothesis tests the impact on actionable decision metrics in imbalanced settings.
data.statement: In imbalanced tabular classification tasks, post-hoc calibration (isotonic or Platt) leads to a significant improvement in top-decile precision and a reduction in false negatives (FN), especially when business risk constraints (e.g., FN ≫ FP) are prioritized.

data.rationale: The hypothesis compares isotonic regression and Platt scaling in improving calibration (ECE) in tree ensembles on imbalanced tabular data. To test this, we select two imbalanced datasets—breast_cancer_imb10 and digits_binary_imb10—that mirror real-world class imbalance. The control condition uses random_forest+platt, representing the baseline calibration method. The treatment condition uses random_forest+isotonic, testing whether isotonic regression improves ECE more than Platt scaling. We focus on ECE (dependent variable) and AUC (to monitor discrimination cost), using paired Wilcoxon test to assess significant differences between methods. Five-fold cross-validation ensures robustness, and three random seeds ensure reproducibility and reduce variance. The choice of imbalanced datasets (with minority class reduced to 10%) directly addresses the gap G3, which points to a lack of systematic comparison under class imbalance. Random forest is selected as the tree ensemble model due to its prevalence and relevance in tabular data. The design controls for model type and dataset structure, isolating the effect of calibration method.

The hypothesis focuses on post-hoc calibration in imbalanced tabular settings with business risk constraints (FN ≫ FP), where top-decile precision and false negative rate are critical. We select two imbalanced datasets—breast_cancer_imb10 and digits_binary_imb10—representing real-world classification tasks with class imbalance (minority class at 10% of majority). The control uses a strong baseline model (gradient boosting), which is known for handling imbalanced data well. The treatment conditions apply Platt and isotonic calibration to assess their impact on actionable metrics. Using gradient boosting as the base ensures consistent model performance while isolating the effect of calibration. Paired Wilcoxon test is used because it is appropriate for non-normal, small-sample comparisons of two related conditions (calibration methods) on the same model base. Five-fold cross-validation with three random seeds ensures reproducibility and robustness in estimating performance under variation. The choice of metrics directly aligns with the hypothesis’s dependent variables and business risk context.
